newsitem.title: FRANCE: French selloff plan for Cr Lyonnais nearly ready.
newsitem.headline: French selloff plan for Cr Lyonnais nearly ready.

text.p: After numerous delays, France's plan to privatise state-owned bank Credit Lyonnais is nearly ready and should be sent to the European Commission for clearance soon, a finance ministry official said on Wednesday.
"The plan is almost finished. It should be sent to Brussels very soon but there is no precise date," the official said.
The Commission, which must clear all state aid, is expected to get the plan at the end of the month or in early June after the French parliamentary election.
The ruling centre-right coalition is tipped to win the election, although it is not certain the same finance ministry team will be in place after the vote.

The plan, which was due to go to Commission competition authorities in February, had been the subject of heated talks between Credit Lyonnais and the government over what sacrifices the bank should make in return for state help ahead of its sale.

The bank, which almost collapsed in the early 1990s under the weight of its lending excesses before being bailed out by massive amounts of state aid, was unwilling to countenance any measures that might jeopardise its viability.
But now the bank and the government had reached accord, a source close to the talks said. "There is an agreement between the finance ministry and the government," the source said.

Finance Minister Jean Arthuis, who said last month the government would not recapitalise Lyonnais ahead of the sale in late 1998 or early 1999, said on Wednesday some money could be forthcoming at the time of its disposal.
"If it were to have problems with its (solvency) ratio at the time of the privatisation it could have recourse to market operations," he told reporters, without being more specific.

The bank's Tier One ratio is 4.6, below the French average of 6.0, and Lyonnais had argued that it needed to be higher to attract a buyer. Disposals under the privatisation plan will change the ratio by altering the bank's parameters.
Still, the source said: "There will probably be another financial effort but the way the recapitalisation will be carried out has not been established."

Newspaper reports have said that the bank, which has staged an unexpectedly strong recovery and is expected to post profits of around two billion francs ($350 million) in 1997 and nearly three billion in 1998, could be sold for at least 25 billion francs.
Lyonnais lost 21 billion francs between 1992 and 1994 before edging back into the black in 1995 with a profit of 13 million francs. It had a profit of 202 million in 1996.
The privatisation plan is expected to involve the disposal of most of the bank's European assets outside France to meet EC conditions for approval of state aid.
The government plans to neutralise the cost of a loan granted by Lyonnais under a previous state bailout to finance the spinoff of dud assets from its balance sheet.
"The idea is to keep Credit Lyonnais a universal bank in France and let it keep its business banking and capital markets presence in Asia, Eastern Europe and the U.S.," the source said.

The bank has high hopes of its U.S., Eastern European and Asian operations. Last year, the United States showed 1.2 billion francs in profits while Asia generated 800 million and Eastern Europe 200 million.
The Commission is expected to take several months to decide on the privatisation plan.
-- Penny MacRae, Paris Newsroom +33 1 4221 5452 ($ = 5.742 French Francs)
